prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Ito, Tokyo, Hadn

outputs.L1:
Ito ran to a window.  
He danced. He howled.  
He cursed the moon,  
interned in a camp before  
being carted onto a ship  
bound for Tokyo.  

Had he not nearly died for art  
on evenings when he ate bread soup?  
If he wished to forget those days  
and nights dancing in drawing rooms  
in London, or translating Fenollosa’s  
notes on Noh, he would have to unbraid  
himself from *At the Hawk’s Well*,  
and then relinquish the Egyptian  
mask Dulac had painted him into—  
claws, beak, feathers, and legend.  

Why had that foolish boy told a story  
of his grandmother weeping  
when she first saw him dressed  
in his grandfather’s samurai armor,  
all to hold the gaze of Lady Cunard?  

Once more, he was studying the fox  
holding a biscuit in his hand,  
saying, “I went to a great hill  
in Hampstead, and I made my soul  
into the soul of a fox.”  

At last, he would release his Europe,  
and no longer think of those he loved  
and taught, Isadora lost.  

Now, powerless and alone,  
he dances his ten steps  
again and again,  
wanting to know whether a hawk  
could peck the eyes from a fox.
outputs.L2:
Ito hurried toward the window.  
He moved in a dance.  
He cried out like an animal.  
He reviled the moon,  
after being held in a camp  
before they put him aboard a vessel  
and sent him back to Tokyo.

Had he not nearly given his life to art  
on those nights when his meal was bread soup?  
If he wanted to erase the memory  
of those days and evenings performing in London salons,  
or of rendering Fenollosa’s Noh notes into English,  
he would first need to disentangle himself  
from *At the Hawk’s Well*,  
and then surrender the Egyptian face  
Dulac had turned him into—  
talons, hooked beak, plumage, and myth.

Why had that foolish young man recounted  
how his grandmother cried  
the first time she saw him wearing  
his grandfather’s samurai armor,  
just to keep Lady Cunard’s attention fixed on him?

Once more he considered the fox,  
a biscuit held in its paw,  
declaring, “I climbed a high hill  
in Hampstead, and I transformed my soul  
into the soul of a fox.”

At last,  
he would relinquish Europe  
and stop dwelling on the people  
he had loved and instructed,  
with Isadora gone.

Now, stripped of power and by himself,  
he repeats his ten steps  
over and over,  
trying to discover whether a hawk  
might tear out a fox’s eyes.
outputs.L3:
Ito is portrayed in a moment of deep anguish, cursing the moon as memories of his past return to him. He recalls the humiliation and fear of being interned before eventually being sent back to Tokyo, a return that feels less like a homecoming than an exile. In this state of distress, his mind moves between personal suffering and artistic memory, showing how closely his identity has become tied to performance.

He reflects on the sacrifices he made in the name of art. His career was not built on ease or comfort, but on hardship, hunger, displacement, and relentless effort. He remembers the years he spent in Europe performing, translating, adapting, and shaping himself into an artist who could move between cultures. These sacrifices gave him recognition, but they also left him vulnerable, as though his life had been consumed by the very art he served.

At the same time, Ito struggles to separate himself from the artistic identities he has taken on. The roles he performed have become inseparable from his sense of self, particularly his association with *At the Hawk’s Well* and the imagery of Edmund Dulac’s Egyptian-inspired mask. These figures and symbols cling to him, suggesting that performance has not merely represented him but has begun to possess him. He cannot easily tell where Ito the man ends and Ito the artist begins.

His memories also return to the European audiences before whom he repeatedly fashioned himself into different stories and personas. He recalls performing for figures such as Lady Cunard, offering himself as an object of fascination and interpretation. Among these transformations is his assumption of the soul of a fox, a figure of cunning, enchantment, and otherness. Through such performances, Ito became both artist and spectacle, admired yet exoticized, powerful on stage yet dependent on the gaze of others.

In the end, he is left alone and powerless, repeating his dance steps as if they are the last remaining proof of who he is. The movements that once brought him artistic authority now become gestures of uncertainty and survival. As he dances, he wonders whether the hawk can destroy the fox, a question that suggests an inner conflict between the roles, symbols, and selves that have defined him. His anguish lies not only in exile or defeat, but in the terrifying possibility that the art to which he gave his life may also be capable of consuming him.
outputs.L4:
Ito’s exile, artistic identity, and painful memories are explored through a series of fragmented images that move between performance, myth, and recollection. Rather than presenting his life as a clear narrative, the poem suggests his inner state through broken scenes and symbolic gestures. Ito appears as a figure caught between cultures and histories, someone who has carried the marks of Europe with him even as he tries to escape them. His art becomes the place where these tensions are revealed: the stage is not only a space of beauty and movement, but also a space where memory, displacement, and grief return again and again.

The poem shows Ito attempting to shed his European past, but it also makes clear that this past cannot simply be abandoned. Its symbols continue to surround him and shape the way he understands himself. Mythic references and theatrical images give his struggle a larger meaning, suggesting that his personal exile is also a kind of spiritual and artistic crisis. His repeated dance becomes more than a performance; it becomes a ritual of remembering and resisting. Each movement seems to express both survival and loss, as if he is trying to transform pain into art while knowing that the pain cannot fully disappear.

In this way, the poem presents Ito as a haunted figure. He is not only remembering what has been lost, but also questioning who he is after that loss. His dance is powerful because it contains contradiction: it is an act of endurance, but also a sign of entrapment; it is a way to continue living, but also a return to wounds that remain unresolved. Through its fractured imagery and symbolic language, the poem portrays art as a means of survival, while also showing the limits of art’s ability to heal. Ito’s performance ultimately becomes a haunting expression of exile, memory, and the search for identity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about Michio Ito in exile, reflecting on his internment, deportation to Tokyo, his collaborations with Yeats and Dulac, and the imagery of hawks, foxes, masks, and dance.
counterfactuals.output:
**Michio Ito in Exile**

In the desert barracks  
the body remembers what the nation forgets.

A wrist lifts—  
not quite a wing,  
not quite a plea.

Outside the wire,  
America rehearses its fear  
with rifles, papers, names mispronounced.  
Inside, a dancer folds the air  
into angles no guard can confiscate.

He has been othered before:  
in London fog,  
in Paris rooms,  
on stages where the East  
was both mirror and mask,  
summoned, admired, misunderstood.

Yeats heard the hawk in him—  
that stillness before the strike,  
that godlike bird  
waiting beside the well  
where no one drinks without becoming  
less human, more myth.

Dulac painted the face  
that was not a face:  
lacquered silence,  
a mask with the moon behind it,  
eyes cut open  
for spirits to look through.

And Ito moved there,  
between Noh and modernity,  
between invocation and invention,  
his steps spare as calligraphy,  
each pause a dark brushstroke  
on the white paper of the stage.

But now the stage is dust.  
Now the spotlight is a watchtower.  
Now the music is boots,  
keys, orders, the clack  
of a train taking him eastward  
toward the Pacific,  
toward deportation,  
toward Tokyo burning in the distance  
of history’s next catastrophe.

What does a dancer carry  
when stripped of country?

A hawk’s patience.  
A fox’s cunning.  
The memory of masks  
hung like ancestors  
in the theater of the mind.

The fox slips under fences  
made of law.  
The hawk circles above maps  
drawn by men who fear the sky.

Ito, in exile,  
does not stop moving.

Even seated, he dances:  
shoulder, breath, eyelid, hand.  
Even silenced, he composes  
with the grammar of tendon and bone.

Tokyo receives him  
not as home receives a son,  
but as war receives the displaced—  
with sirens, hunger, ash,  
with the old gods crowded  
into cellars and stations.

Still, somewhere,  
a mask waits for a face.  
A sleeve waits for wind.  
A foot waits for the floor  
to become water.

He thinks of Yeats,  
of the well guarded by the hawk;  
of Dulac’s colors drying  
into legend;  
of audiences who saw beauty  
and called it foreign,  
then foreignness  
and called it danger.

He lifts his arms.

For a moment  
the room is not a room.  
The war is not the war.  
The exile is not exile.

A hawk descends.  
A fox turns back  
at the edge of the field.  
The mask opens its wooden mouth.

And the dancer,  
deported, interned, renamed by suspicion,  
steps lightly through the ruin—  
not escaping history,  
but making from its cage  
one more impossible  
dance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense literary poem in the style of a biographical fragment, centered on Japanese dancer Michio Ito remembering London, Noh theater, At the Hawk’s Well, Isadora Duncan, and his wartime removal from the West.
counterfactuals.output:
**Fragment for Michio Ito**

In London I learned to be weather:  
fog at the collar, coal-smoke in the lung,  
the Thames turning its dull blade under bridges  
while Europe, with one hand gloved in etiquette,  
felt for the pulse of Asia in my wrist.

I had brought no temple, only the hinge  
of the knee, the grave arithmetic of a sleeve,  
the fan’s small moon opening above silence.  
Noh was not a mask but a discipline of distance:  
to cross a stage as if crossing a life already ended,  
to lift the foot and let centuries pass beneath it,  
to make the body a bell whose sound is withheld.

Yeats watched the hawk descend into the well of air.  
Pound sharpened the light; the room became ritual.  
At the Hawk’s Well—stone, thirst, bird, old man, hero—  
I stood inside a borrowed myth and found it strangely native:  
the Irish wind entered by way of the Japanese drum,  
and language, unable to follow, knelt at the threshold.  
My hands remembered what the poem had not yet said.

Before this, Isadora had flung open the West  
like a window in a fever ward.  
Barefoot, she made Greece a verb,  
made the torso a republic, made music visible.  
I watched freedom learn its own weight  
and knew that even flight must be measured  
if it is to remain in the world.

Then the maps darkened.  
Names became borders, faces became evidence.  
The country that had applauded the arc of my arm  
counted my blood as contraband.  
Wartime came with its bureaucratic winter,  
its trains, its lists, its locked horizons;  
the West removed me from itself  
as if plucking a note from a chord  
could save the song from dissonance.

What remains is not exile only.  
It is the pause before the drumbeat,  
the mask turned slightly toward an unseen shore,  
London burning in memory’s lacquer,  
the hawk still circling its impossible water,  
Isadora’s footfall fading into surf,  
and my body—brief nation, disciplined flame—  
walking again through fog,  
each step a biography,  
each silence an arrival.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an ekphrastic modernist poem about Michio Ito as the Hawk in Yeats’s At the Hawk’s Well, haunted by Europe, internment, samurai ancestry, Lady Cunard, and a fox-soul ritual on Hampstead Heath.
counterfactuals.output:
**MICHIO ITO AS THE HAWK**

A mask, but not a mask—  
the face sharpened backward into beak,  
the wrist becoming weather.

At the well that will not fill  
Yeats listens for Ireland  
and hears instead  
a Japanese footfall on London boards,  
dry as a twig in Noh twilight.

Ito stands there:  
man / bird / blade,  
a hinge in the air.  
His sleeve is a wing refusing wind.  
His eye, black lacquer,  
keeps the old water sleepless.

Europe coughs behind the curtain—  
Paris with its absinthe lamps,  
Berlin’s iron throat,  
the trenches under the music,  
the violin-string nerves of 1916.  
Civilization, in evening dress,  
has blood on its gloves.

Lady Cunard’s drawing room glitters—  
silver, scandal, porcelain talk—  
while the dancer lowers one shoulder  
and a continent falls through it.  
The guests admire “Japan,”  
that exquisite wound  
folded into a fan.

But under the silk:  
a clan-mark, a ghost-helmet,  
samurai grandfathers in lacquered rain.  
Their swords sleep badly.  
They ring in his tendons  
when he holds still.

Hold still—  
the hawk is not still.  
The stillness is the strike  
before the strike.

Later: barbed wire, America,  
the polite machinery of suspicion.  
A name becomes a cage.  
An accent becomes evidence.  
The body that crossed empires  
is counted, tagged, removed.  
Even the hawk  
must learn the geometry of fences.

Yet on Hampstead Heath, before all that—  
moon thin as a shaved bone,  
grass wet with London’s secret animal breath—  
someone draws a circle.  
Someone whispers kitsune,  
fox-fire, fox-bride, fox-soul.  
A bowl, a thread, a bell.  
A ritual too old  
or too invented  
to be false.

Ito turns.

Not the hawk now—  
or not only.  
The fox enters the ankle first,  
then the spine.  
The heath tilts.  
The city’s chimneys blacken like burnt incense.  
Europe watches from the fog,  
wearing all its dead faces.

He dances possession  
without surrender:  
heel, claw, fan, blade,  
the beautiful refusal of belonging.  
Ireland’s well. Japan’s theater.  
England’s lawn.  
America’s camp.  
All of them thirsting  
at the same stone mouth.

O Hawk, O Ito,  
split emblem, immigrant star—  
you do not fly from history.  
You pin it under your talon  
and make it look up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a historical persona poem in which Michio Ito, after being interned and sent back to Japan, tries to shed his European artistic identity and repeats a dance while thinking of hawks, foxes, Fenollosa, Dulac, and lost friends.
counterfactuals.output:
**Michio Ito, Repatriated**

I have unbuttoned Europe from my sleeves.  
Still, its pale cuffs cling to the wrist—  
Dalcroze in the metronome of bone,  
the London rooms, the painted masks,  
Dulac’s blue shadows folding behind my eyes  
like screens I cannot store away.

Again, I begin the step.

Heel—  
pause—  
the hand lifts, not as a hand  
but as a hawk remembering height.  
The shoulder turns.  
The fox enters under the ribs,  
quick flame, sly grief,  
a village rumor moving through snow.

They sent me back across the water  
as if a man were only address,  
as if the sea could rinse him clean  
of theaters, friends, applause,  
of those who took my name in English  
and made from it a lamp.

Again, I begin.

Fenollosa whispers from a dead page:  
Japan is not behind you.  
It waits where the brush has not yet touched.  
But what is “Japan” to one  
who has carried too many mirrors?  
I bow, and hear California wire.  
I rise, and smell the ship’s iron breath.

Hawk—  
fox—  
stillness—  
turn.

I try to loosen the foreign music,  
to let it fall like a borrowed coat.  
Yet even naked, I am layered:  
Noh dusk, Paris ankle,  
Tokyo dust, London fog,  
the lost faces seated in the dark  
where no curtain lifts.

Again. Again.

The body repeats  
what history cannot forgive.  
The foot returns to earth  
as if asking permission.  
The hand cuts air  
as if opening a door.

Hawk above me,  
fox within me,  
old friends beyond the stage-light—  
watch:  
I am not shedding one skin  
but dancing until every skin  
becomes motion.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, compressed poem with no explanatory context about a Japanese performer named Ito, using references to Noh, London drawing rooms, bread soup, Egyptian masks, Lady Cunard, Isadora, and the question of whether a hawk can blind a fox.
counterfactuals.output:
Ito lifts the Noh moon—  
a sleeve, a bell, a breath.

In London drawing rooms  
tea cools beside bread soup;  
Lady Cunard leans  
toward an Egyptian mask  
and hears Japan click open  
like a fan of bone.

Isadora’s bare foot  
remembers thunder.  
Ito’s painted stillness  
cuts the lamps in two.

Who asks, after midnight,  
whether a hawk can blind a fox?  
The answer wears no face,  
only gold,  
only silence,  
only flight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
